newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire appeals to U.N. over "external aggression".
newsitem.headline: Zaire appeals to U.N. over "external aggression".

text.p: Zaire has appealed to the U.N. Security Council over what it termed "external agression" in its eastern region, state radio said on Thursday.
"Zaire has lodged a complaint with the U.N. Security Council regarding the war between the Banyamulenge and the Zairean army," the Voice of Zaire said.
Zairean troops pulled back towards the South Kivu provincial capital Bukavu on Thursday as Banyamulenge guerrillas were reported to have seized two towns between Bukavu and Uvira.

Zaire accuses neighbouring Burundi and Rwanda, whose armies are dominated by Tutsis, of helping the Banyamulenge Tutsis who settled from Rwanda 200 years ago and are locked in conflict with native Zaireans. Both countries deny the charges.
The radio said deputy foreign minister Lokondo Yoka had briefed ambassadors of the three nations with the greatest clout in the region -- Belgium, France and the United States.
"The Banyamulenge affair is not an internal rebellion as certain people would like it to be known," the radio quoted Lokondo as saying after meeting the envoys on Wednesday.
"Rather, it is an external aggression. For the Banyamulenge have lived in Zaire for decades without rising up against the established authority," he said.
The minister said the legal framework existed for resolving the biter dispute over the Banyamulenge's nationality, which is at the root of the conflict.
In other diplomatic moves by Zaire, Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo was due to meet Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene in Brussels on Thursday to discuss the conflict in eastern Zaire.
"He is coming to Brussels in the framework of a European trip. He asked several hours ago to be received by the prime minister," Moniek Delvou, Dehaene's spokeswoman, said.
Zaire says the Banyamulenge are Rwandan and the latest warfare exploded over attempts by the army and local authorities to force them out. The Banyamulenge insist they are Zairean.
Ethnic rivalries in eastern Zaire were heightened by the influx in mid-1994 of more than a million Hutu refugees from the civil war and massacres in Rwanda at the time.
Rwanda has accused Zaireans and their Hutu allies of planning a genocide of Banyamulenge Tutsis like the 1994 massacres in Rwanda of up to a million minority Tutsis and their sympathisers by Hutus.
An exiled Rwandan Hutu lobby group alleged in Kenya on Thursday that 1,800 Rwandan troops were fighting alongside Banyamulenge rebels in eastern Zaire.
Rwanda swiftly denied the accusation, saying military advances by the Banyamulenge this week were an indication of gross incompetence by the Zairean military.
